1:
The opening word decides the tone of the speech. Clarke gives the Hebrew and renders it a question whether there is not a warfare to miserable man upon earth, and most versions took it so. Henry slips the same gloss into a parenthesis, that the word is warfare. Delitzsch is most exact, that the noun means not the labour of a field hand but active military service and so toil generally, and he corrects Ewald and others for rendering the following line as though it spoke of a slave. Gill alone keeps the received sense of an appointed time, a set term for coming into the world and going out of it, which he confines to earth, since neither heaven nor hell has a limited time to offer.

Henry and Wesley agree on what Job is doing here: excusing what he cannot justify, his longing for death. Henry has him head off the objection in advance: the desire is not a claim that the time appointed of God can be anticipated, only language in which present uneasiness expresses itself. Wesley puts it as a question, whether it is a crime to wish God would bring him to that joyful period. Henry also makes something of the setting: a man on the earth is meanly placed beside the inhabitants of higher regions yet shown mercy in the place itself, being on the earth and not under it, and time here is short according to the narrow bounds of this earth, whereas heaven cannot be measured.

What the servant longs for is read three ways. Gill takes it of shade from the midday heat and notes that the verb means to gape or pant after it. Clarke thinks night is meant and supports it from Virgil and his commentator, who observes that it makes no difference whether one says shadow or night, night being the shadow of the earth. Wesley shortens it to sunset. Delitzsch states the comparison Job was heading for, death as a labourer's rest, and observes that he does not quite reach it.

The nights are where the figure turns against itself, and Gill sees it first. This is not the application of the two similes, he says, because the terms do not answer: instead of the refreshing shadow Job has months of vanity, and instead of the labourer's sweet sleep, wearisome nights. Clarke keeps the military half running, a man like a soldier harassed by the enemy and always on the watch. Ellicott supplies a rendering that catches the restlessness: the night is long and he is filled with tossings to and fro until the morning twilight.

On the body the commentary turns clinical. Ellicott names the disease: it is characteristic of elephantiasis for the skin to grow hard and rugged, then crack and ulcerate. Clarke thinks the worms no figure but literal, insects having laid eggs in open sores, and breaks off because the image is too horrid to pursue; on the second phrase he says outright that all the commentators have missed the sense, which he takes for the crusts of dried matter that flake from decaying pustules. Gill rejects the reading that makes this the corruption of the grave and canvasses the vermicular or pedicular disease; Wesley has the worms bred from the sores and the dust that on which the sufferer lay. The closing image raises a question of antiquities: Clarke notes the word means the weaver rather than his shuttle, doubts whether such an instrument existed then, cites an account of Aleppo where fine cloth was woven with every thread passed by hand, yet concludes something of the kind must have been in view or the figure loses its force. Gill notes that some versions make it a racer and that the Greek wrongly gives swifter than speech; Wesley says only that the shuttle crosses the web in a moment.
7:
Henry notices the change of address and explains it shrewdly. Job, seeing his friends will not interrupt but have stopped attending, turns from them to God, since if men will not hear us God will, and if men cannot help us he can. Henry then enters the caveat that governs the speech: we must not go to school to Job to learn how to speak to God, there being a great mixture of passion and corruption in what he says, yet if God is not extreme to mark what his people say amiss, neither should we be. What Job asks, on this reading, is that God will either ease him or end him.

The figure for life is read as breath rather than storm. Gill takes the word so, a man's life sitting in his nostrils and being a vapour or a bubble, though he allows the other sense too, noisy and blusterous and gone. Henry keeps both halves, life being like the wind in seeming loud but proving empty, soon gone and past recall, and recalls that God had compassion on Israel by remembering they were but flesh. Clarke reports an alternative rendering in which the loss dreaded is not life but the sight of former mercies, and declines it, the common translation giving a very good sense.

The next line is the sharpest in the passage and several render it alike. Delitzsch translates it as a broken sentence, thine eyes look for me and I am no more; Ellicott gives the same sense, God's own eyes seeking him and he not there, with the Greek and Latin behind it. Wesley makes it more terrible still, that one angry look would suffice, since God can look a man into eternity. Clarke offers two constructions, either that God can look him into nothing, or that the look is the sentence of a man already judged to death. Gill enters a qualification the others omit, that this must be limited to human sight, since the dead are still seen by the eyes of the omniscient God, in heaven, in hell and in the grave.

Over the cloud the comment is admiring. Ellicott calls it a fine simile and says why it is apt: whether a summer cloud thins away on the face of the sky or comes down in rain, nothing passes more completely, being an appearance only that comes to nothing. Gill notes the Targum reads smoke instead, and heads off an objection, that although clouds are elsewhere said to return after rain those are not the same clouds; the same figure, he adds, serves for pardon. Wesley turns it into an observation from life, that when a cloud which looked great enough to eclipse the sun is suddenly dispersed, that is exactly the life of man. Clarke states the comparison flatly: as the cloud never returns, neither do the dead return to the living.

The last verse raises the question of how much may be built on it, and Ellicott is careful. These words need not be forced into a denial that Job believed in a future life, because on any view they are accurately true of man as we know him here: even if he lives again elsewhere, it is not in this world, and this world is what Job speaks of. Clarke says the same more briefly, that annihilation is not meant but only that the man will never again inhabit earth, and notes that the word rendered grave covers the state of the dead, any deep pit, and sometimes hell. Gill takes the house literally and figuratively, the second being the earthly house of the body, to which its tenant does not return until the resurrection rebuilds it. Wesley draws the practical inference, that it concerns us to secure a better place, since this one will own us no more.
11:
Gill sets out the reasoning behind the decision to speak: the common lot is warfare enough, extraordinary afflictions have been added, no good is to be had in the present life, and he is going where no temporal good can be expected and from which there is no returning. Clarke reduces it to a sentence, that all is hopeless and he will indulge himself in complaining. Wesley reads it as intention rather than surrender, that Job will plead with God for pity before he dies and ease himself by pouring out his complaint instead of smothering it.

The verse about the sea is the hardest here. Ellicott says the reasonable course is to explain it from Scripture if possible, and finds the key in the prophet's picture of sand set as a bound for the sea; he adds that a writer familiar with Egypt would know the Nile, still called the sea, as a thing watched and diked so its overflow should not ruin the land. Clarke reports the Targum, which asks whether Job is condemned as the Egyptians drowned in the Red Sea or as Pharaoh in his sins, offers his own paraphrases, whether the speaker is as dangerous as the sea that it must be fenced or an ungovernable beast to be kept behind bars, and concludes that the received English is less exceptionable than any rendering yet offered. Delitzsch translates it as sea or sea-monster with a watch set over him. Gill takes the comparison morally, the restless sea standing for abandoned sinners and the raging sea for persecutors, and answers that Job was the reverse of both, gentle to the poor and their rescuer. Wesley draws the application, that in affliction we are apt to complain as though more were laid on us than there is occasion for, whereas we are never in heaviness but when there is need, nor more than there is need.

On the dreams Gill offers three causes without choosing: the distemper breaking his sleep and disturbing the imagination, the melancholy his afflictions had brought on, or Satan, in whose hands he had been placed. Clarke has no such hesitation, holding that Satan was certainly permitted to haunt the imagination, so that the sufferer needed sleep and was afraid to close his eyes for the images waiting there, and asks whether a state more deplorable can be conceived.

Whether suicide is in view divides them sharply. Ellicott renders the line literally as choosing death rather than these my bones, notes that some take it as a death by these my members, and glosses that as a death inflicted by himself. Gill denies it outright: not to strangle himself as Ahithophel did, nor strangling as a judicial execution, but, following Broughton, to be choked by some suffocating disease, since death in any form is the stopping of a man's breath, which is what Job wanted. Clarke takes a third route, that in those broken slumbers he felt an oppression like the nightmare and would have preferred death that way to longer life in such misery.

The closing phrase gets three readings from Ellicott alone, the thing loathed being the thought of self-destruction, or life itself, or, less probably, a wasting away; he then re-reads the next clause against the received version, preferring I shall not live for ever as suiting the context better than I would not live always, so the line arrives as a ray of comfort rather than a refusal. Clarke keeps the refusal and sharpens it, that length of days offered on these terms would be a boon to be spurned, and he reports another rendering in which the soul covets suffocation and asks for release. Gill offers his own alternatives, that the loathing falls on life or on his bones, or that the sense is rather I am become loathsome, or, being ulcerated, I pine away.
17:
The question about man divides the witnesses by tone. Henry sets out both possibilities without choosing: either a passionate reflection on divine justice, as though the great God disparaged himself by contending with a creature so far beneath him, or a pious admiration of condescending grace like Psalm 8:4. Clarke frames the same alternative and adds the paraphrase of Calmet, in which Job protests that he is not worthy that God should concern himself about him. Wesley takes only the first, that man is not worthy of God's favour and is below his anger. Gill takes only the second, marvelling that God should magnify a frail and fallen creature at all, and reading the magnifying as election and espousal to his Son.

On the morning visitation Gill lets both senses stand and observes that the argument comes out the same either way: God visits in mercy, as the dayspring from on high and in mercies renewed every morning, or he visits in punishment, which for his own people is fatherly chastisement. Henry supplies the pictures, the daily call on a particular friend and the physician's round, and reads the trying every moment as feeling the pulse and observing the looks. Wesley widens the trial beyond affliction to prosperity and blessing.

The swallowing of the spittle is read two ways. Clarke calls it proverbial, still current among the Arabs in nearly the same language, and equivalent to asking for the twinkling of an eye; Ellicott agrees it is doubtless proverbial, and Wesley glosses it as a breathing time. Henry takes it as description rather than proverb, supposing Job's distemper lay much in his throat and almost choked him, and citing his later complaint that it bound him about like the collar of his coat.

Whether Job here confesses is the sharpest division in the chapter. Henry reads a plain and ingenuous confession, and makes the point that God had called him perfect while he says of himself that he has sinned, so a man may be upright who is not sinless. Gill notes that some supply an if, refuses the supplement, and keeps it an affirmation, though of ordinary daily sin rather than of the notorious course his friends alleged. Delitzsch settles it the other way on grammatical grounds, marking the clause hypothetical, so the sense is granted that I have sinned; Ellicott renders it the same way, putting the case that I have sinned. Clarke reports Kennicott's proposal that the words are addressed to Eliphaz rather than to God, and argues from Bildad's reply, which answers a man justifying himself, that Job does not criminate himself here; otherwise, he says, the controversy would have ended and the book with it.

The clauses that follow divide on text as well as sense. Ellicott keeps the burden on Job himself and offers two figures for the mark, either a target on which God expends all his arrows or a stumbling-block he comes into collision against. Delitzsch reads the line as a burden to Thee instead. Henry hears the divine title two ways, observer and preserver, noting that observer aggravates the confession while preserver is the right thing to plead in repentance.

On the prayer for pardon Gill takes lift up literally and traces the lifting from the sinner to the Son and away by blood. Ellicott explains the urgency from Job's premise that sin was the origin of all disaster, so pardon would end the sorrow, and adds that our Lord did not discourage the belief when he joined the assurance of forgiveness to the healing of the paralytic in Matthew 9:2. Henry draws the doctrinal point that where God removes the guilt of sin he breaks its power, and reads the plea from the near prospect of the grave: those who cannot sleep on a bed of down will shortly sleep in a bed of dust.
